title: proto.c: `proto_tree_add_mac48_detail()` function
description:
Create a public function in `epan/proto.c` to dissect a single MAC-48
address. Encapsulates the name and OUI resolution, and the LG and IG
bit parsing.

Created after observing that `packet-ieee80211.c` does not resolve the
OUI or IG/LG bits for WLAN fields (`wlan.ra`, `wlan.da`, `wlan.sa`,
`wlan.bssid`) the way that `packet-eth.c` does.

This change modifies `packet-eth.c` and `packet-ieee80211.c` to use the new function.

changed this line in [version 3 of the diff](/wireshark/wireshark/-/merge_requests/11967/diffs?diff_id=783262990&start_sha=b3eb4b37ee44a0b691fc61d0893891a1b848267a#b803cae5b87b977149769f3fa810595aceaf61e7_624_620)
Changed to `hf_list`.

There's nothing specific to IEEE 802.3 in `dissect_eth_address()`, so it probably belongs somewhere else, e.g. epan/proto.c.

And non-dissector-specific routines to add fields to the protocol tree tend to have names of the form `proto_tree_add_XXX`, so perhaps `proto_tree_add_eth_address()`?

(And, yes, at some point we might want to speak of MAC-48 addresses rather than Ethernet addresses, e.g. `FT_MAC48` and `mac48` replacing `eth` in stuff that's not Ethernet-specific; I recently did a similar rename in tcpdump's source.)

Most of the `proto_tree_add_XXX` functions do a lot less work than is being done by this new function, which adds up to twelve items to the tree with one call. I'm fine with `proto_tree_add_eth_address()` or `proto_tree_add_mac48_address()` if you are, it just seems like a slightly different beast.
Moved to proto.c and renamed `proto_tree_add_mac48_detail().`

It strikes me that this function could probably be trivially expanded to also work for EUI-64 addresses, since the OUI, LG, and IG are in the same places (relative to the start of the address) as for MAC-48.

As I look at using this new function in `proto-ieee80211.c` I see that my approach, if naïvely applied, will result in some duplicate fields for the hidden 'generic' address fields `wlan.addr` and `wlan.addr_resolved`. For example, in a 802.11 beacon, the first address is marked as both receiver and destination (`wlan.ra` and `wlan.da`); the dissector only adds one `wlan.addr` for this, but my approach would add two.

There's also a memory impact for this approach. To prevent passing all the desired fields as arguments to `proto_tree_add_mac48_detail()`, I create a static struct which holds fourteen pointers, or 112 bytes, per MAC address. Looking again at `proto-ieee80211.c` that's an added 672 bytes of RAM set aside in case someone dissects some WLAN traffic.

(values given assume 64-bit pointers)

I've changed it so the `mac_hf_list_t` is smaller, and you pass two of them to the function: one for the specific type of address (such as destination), and one for the generic address information. (They're now passed as pointers, too.) Benefits:

1. The generic list can be reused, instead of taking space in multiple structs to hold the same information
2. The generic list can be passed as NULL, and those items won't be added
 
Going back to `proto-ieee80211.c` as an example, we'd need seven structs instead of six, but each is less than half the size it was in my first iteration.
On the positive side, this new function could conceivably also be used for EUI-64 addresses, since the OUI (and thus LG and IG bits) are in the first three bytes of both EUI-64 and MAC-48 addresses.
